course_description:
In this course, we examine the long tradition of writings about the Jewish and Christian religions: meditations on the nature of the divine, literary encounters with heaven and hell, and critical reflections on the place of religion in Western society. Through a selection of works designed to show a diversity of perspectives, we explore the ways in which writers have imagined the Jewish and Christian traditions, encountered life through the lens of their faith, and wrestled with the ever-changing role of religion in the West. This course also includes artistic works (musical and visual) that respond to these ideas and a broad exploration of the history of Judaism and Christianity from antiquity to the present.

BAdvHum(Hons) students taking this course as an elective please email westernciv@uq.edu.au to enable your enrolment.

restrictions: Restricted to students enrolled in the BAdvHum(Hons) and BHum/LLB(Hons). Maximum enrolment quota of 60 students.

course_aims:
After successfully completing this course you should be able to:

LO1. Critically and reflectively engage with Western religious traditions. LO2. Think beyond received narratives about Western religious traditions. LO3. Reason and justify individual interpretations of texts in Western religious traditions. LO4. Directly engage with a text in the Jewish religious tradition. LO5. Directly engage with a text in the Christian religious tradition.

assessment_details.title: Close Reading Essay
assessment_details.task_description: You are required to undertake a close reading of one of the assigned passages from the Bible. You must write a 1,500-word analysis of your chosen passage that avoids to the greatest extent possible the interpolation of later, non-historicist elements of interpretation. Your close reading should offer a coherent analysis of the meaning of the passage in its own historical context rather than your own interpretation of it. To do this, you must use the Oxford Annotated Bible version of your chosen passage, carry out independent research, citing a minimum of 6 academic sources, and write an articulate and properly referenced essay. Please be aware that this assessment task is designed to evaluate students’ abilities, skills, and knowledge without the aid of Artificial Intelligence (AI). All gobbet passages will be derived from the books studied in this course. In the second section, you must write an essay in response to 1 of the 5 prompts. learning_activities.topic: Ancient Judaism This lecture will explore the origins, history, and founding stories of Judaism from the 2nd millennium BCE to the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

The Pentateuch: Genesis In this tutorial, students will explore the primeval history of divine creation in the first book of the Pentateuch through a close reading, and discuss the significance of Genesis for Western history. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Rabbinic Judaism This lecture will examine the history of Rabbinic Judaism from the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE to the early Middle Ages. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

The Ketuvim: The Book of Job In this tutorial, students will read The Book of Job, exploring its major theme of theodicy – the problem of human suffering and divine justice in the world – through close textual analysis of key passages. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Historical Jesus This lecture will explore the origins of Christianity from the birth of Jesus to the composition of the Gospels. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

The New Testament: The Gospel of Matthew In this tutorial, students will do a close reading of the Gospel of Matthew, exploring the way in which Matthew aligns Jesus with aspects of both Judaism and nascent Christianity. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Church & Empire This lecture will explore the emergence of a catholic form of Christianity in the first four centuries CE, along with the growth of churches in the Mediterranean, and Christianity’s fateful alliance with the Roman Empire in 312 CE. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Anonymous: Beowulf In this tutorial, students will read the Old English epic poem Beowulf , the only surviving manuscript of which was thought to have been composed between c. 975-1025 CE. Attention will be paid to the way that this pagan oral narrative was Christianised by the anonymous scribe who composed it. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05
Heaven, Hell, and Purgatory This lecture will examine the historical development of Heaven, Hell, and Purgatory from Late Antiquity to the High Middle Ages. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Dante: Inferno In this tutorial, students will read the first part of Dante’s Divina Commedia , the Inferno , the journey of Dante and his guide Virgil through the nine levels of Hell, and discuss its theology and historical context. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Medieval Eve This lecture will explore the place of women in European society during the Middle Ages, the types of religious misogyny they faced, as well as some early responses to antifeminism. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Pizan: The Book of the City of Ladies In this tutorial, students will read Christine de Pizan’s 1405 defence of women’s contribution to Western culture through her literary construction of an allegorical city. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

The Renaissance This lecture will explore the fortunes of Christianity in the Renaissance, including the emergence of criticism of the Roman Catholic Church from John Wycliffe, Jan Hus, and the movement known as the Devotio moderna . Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Erasmus: In Praise of Folly In this tutorial, students will read the work that anticipated Luther’s Ninety-Five Theses (1517) and the start of the Reformation, Erasmus’s In Praise of Folly , and discuss its method and critique of late medieval and Renaissance culture. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Protestantism This lecture will explore the theology and impact of reformer Martin Luther, as well as the early spread of Protestantism in Germany and Switzerland. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Milton: Paradise Lost (Part 1) In this tutorial, students will read books I-VI of Milton’s Paradise Lost (1667), an epic poem that retells the biblical fall of Adam and Eve in light of God’s war against Satan. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

The English Reformation This lecture will chronicle the history of the Reformation in England from the 1520s to 1660s, with a particular focus on the influence of Calvinism. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Milton: Paradise Lost (Part 2) In this tutorial, students will read books VII-XII of Milton’s Paradise Lost (1667), an epic poem that retells the biblical fall of Adam and Eve in light of God’s war against Satan. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05
Mid-Semester Break
Course Reading Week There will be no lecture or tutorials this week in WCIV1100.

The Haskalah This lecture will explore the roots of modern Judaism in the Haskalah (Jewish Enlightenment) and the division of Judaism into its three modern denominations (Orthodox, Reform, and Conservative) leading up to the Holocaust. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Levi: If This is a Man In this tutorial, students will read Primo Levi’s recollection of his time in Auschwitz concentration camp and discuss the Holocaust’s significance for Judaism and the place of God in the face of unspeakable acts of evil. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Race and Religion This lecture will explore the importance of Judaism and Christianity to the Civil Rights Movement (1954-1968), with a particular focus on the contributions of Martin Luther King Jr. and Abraham Joshua Heschel. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Heschel: The Sabbath In this seminar, students will read Abraham Joshua Heschel’s reflections on modernity and the meaning of time and space for Jewish life in The Sabbath (1951), as a means to reflect on aspects of Judaism’s encounters with the modern world. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Modern Myths This lecture will explore the relation between myth and Christianity in the 20th century, with a particular focus on the Inklings (C. S. Lewis, J. R. R. Tolkien, and Charles Williams). Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

Shaw: Liturgies of the Wild In this tutorial, students will read mythographer and Christian author Martin Shaw’s Liturgies of the Wild and discuss the relationship between myths, religion, and modernity. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
